title: Timing attacks and side channels
summary: Correct crypto can still leak through how long it takes, what it says when it fails, and what it compresses. Recover a secret byte by byte, then close the leak.

steps.title: An early exit is a leak
body: The obvious way to compare two byte arrays stops at the first difference. Step through it: the guess matches the secret for two bytes, so the loop does **three** comparisons before giving up.

An attacker who can measure how long a check takes learns *how many leading bytes were right*. That turns guessing a 16-byte tag from 2¹²⁸ tries into 16 × 256 = 4,096: try all 256 values of byte 0, keep the one that took longest, move on to byte 1. Real attacks over networks average thousands of measurements per guess, and they work.
Here, a *count* of comparisons stands in for time, so everything stays deterministic.

steps.explain: Each correct leading byte adds one comparison. The attacker reads progress straight off the clock.

steps.title: Naive and constant-time comparison
prompt: Write two comparisons that also report how many byte comparisons they made:
- `bool NaiveEquals(byte[] a, byte[] b, out int compared)`: stop at the first difference.
- `bool ConstantTimeEquals(byte[] a, byte[] b, out int compared)`: always look at **every** byte, accumulating differences with `diff |= a[i] ^ b[i]`, and decide only at the end.

If the lengths differ, both return `false` with `compared = 0` (lengths are not secret; a tag's length is public). In real code, use `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`, which does what your second method does.
starter: bool NaiveEquals(byte[] a, byte[] b, out int compared)
bool ConstantTimeEquals(byte[] a, byte[] b, out int compared)
solution: bool NaiveEquals(byte[] a, byte[] b, out int compared)
bool ConstantTimeEquals(byte[] a, byte[] b, out int compared)
template: Dojo.Check("NaiveEquals: equal arrays", NaiveEquals(dojoS, (byte[])dojoS.Clone(), out var dojoN1) && dojoN1 == 8, $"compared {dojoN1}");
Dojo.Check("NaiveEquals stops at the first difference", !NaiveEquals(dojoS, new byte[] { 10, 20, 99, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0 }, out var dojoN2) && dojoN2 == 3, $"compared {dojoN2}");
Dojo.Check("ConstantTimeEquals: equal arrays", ConstantTimeEquals(dojoS, (byte[])dojoS.Clone(), out var dojoC1) && dojoC1 == 8, $"compared {dojoC1}");
Dojo.Check("ConstantTimeEquals looks at every byte", !ConstantTimeEquals(dojoS, new byte[8], out var dojoC2) && dojoC2 == 8, $"compared {dojoC2}");
Dojo.Check("ConstantTimeEquals catches a difference in the last byte", !ConstantTimeEquals(dojoS, new byte[] { 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 81 }, out _), "said equal");

Dojo.Check("different lengths are unequal, zero comparisons", !ConstantTimeEquals(dojoS, new byte[3], out var dojoC3) && dojoC3 == 0 && !NaiveEquals(dojoS, new byte[3], out var dojoN3) && dojoN3 == 0, "wrong length handling");
hints: `ConstantTimeEquals` has no `break` and no `return` inside the loop.
`diff |= a[i] ^ b[i];` stays 0 only if every pair of bytes was equal.

steps.title: The attack, end to end
body: Here is the full byte-at-a-time attack against a server that checks a secret tag with an early exit. The server answers each guess with whether it was accepted and, through its timing, how many bytes it compared:
if the server compared more than i + 1 bytes   -> byte i is v
(for the last byte: if the server accepted      -> done)

At most 256 guesses per byte. Against a 16-byte HMAC tag that is 4,096 requests: an afternoon. With `FixedTimeEquals` every wrong guess compares all 16 bytes, the count never changes, and the attacker is back to 2¹²⁸.

steps.title: Recover a secret through a timing oracle
prompt: Write `byte[] Recover(Func<byte[], (bool Accepted, int Compared)> oracle, int length)` that finds a secret of `length` bytes using only the oracle, which runs an early-exit comparison of your guess against the secret.

Build the guess one position at a time: for position `i`, try all 256 values; the right one makes the oracle compare **more than `i + 1`** bytes, or, at the last position, accept. The tests count your calls: at most 256 per byte.
starter: byte[] Recover(Func<byte[], (bool Accepted, int Compared)> oracle, int length)
solution: byte[] Recover(Func<byte[], (bool Accepted, int Compared)> oracle, int length)
template: Dojo.Eq("the secret is recovered", dojoSecret, dojoGot);
Dojo.Check("at most 256 guesses per byte", dojoCalls <= 256 * dojoSecret.Length, $"{dojoCalls} calls");
Dojo.Check("far fewer guesses than brute force", dojoCalls < 2000, $"{dojoCalls} calls");
hints: Two loops: positions outside, values 0..255 inside, `break` when the oracle says you got further.
`compared > i + 1` means byte `i` matched and the comparison moved on to byte `i + 1`.

steps.prompt: Which change stops this attack completely?
options: Adding a random delay of 0 to 10 ms to every response
Returning HTTP 404 instead of 401 on failure
Using SHA-512 instead of SHA-256 for the tag
steps.explain: Random delays only add noise, which attackers average away with more requests. A longer tag makes the attack longer but not harder per byte. Only removing the data-dependent timing fixes it.

steps.title: Other side channels
body: A **side channel** is anything other than the intended output that depends on a secret:
- **Timing**: early-exit comparisons, branches and table lookups that depend on key bits (why AES runs on dedicated CPU instructions, AES-NI, not lookup tables).
- **Error messages**: "bad padding" versus "bad MAC" made the **padding oracle** attacks (module 3) possible. Fail with *one* message.
- **Length**: compressing secret data together with attacker-chosen data (CRIME, BREACH) leaks the secret through the compressed size. Encryption hides content, not length.
- **Power, electromagnetic and acoustic** emissions from smart cards and chips, and **cache** timing between processes sharing a CPU (Spectre-class attacks).
You mostly defend by using constant-time library code, giving uniform errors, and not compressing secrets next to attacker input.

items: How long a tag comparison takes
A smart card's power draw while signing
Different error texts for bad padding and bad MAC
The compressed size of a response that mixes a secret with user input
steps.explain: A side channel attacks the *implementation*, not the math. Brute force and factoring attack the math; phishing attacks the people.

steps.title: Fix: errors that tell too much
prompt: This request check leaks in two ways: it compares with an early exit, and its error message says **where** the tag went wrong, which hands the attacker the byte-at-a-time attack without even needing a clock.

Fix `string CheckRequest(byte[] key, string body, byte[] tag)` so it returns `"ok"` for a valid HMAC-SHA256 tag and **exactly** `"error: invalid signature"` for every other case (wrong tag, wrong length), using `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`.
starter: string CheckRequest(byte[] key, string body, byte[] tag)
if (tag.Length != 32) return "error: tag must be 32 bytes";
if (expected[i] != tag[i]) return $"error: tag mismatch at byte {i}";
solution: string CheckRequest(byte[] key, string body, byte[] tag)
template: Dojo.Eq("a valid tag is ok", "ok", CheckRequest(dojoKey, "GET /orders", dojoTag));
Dojo.Eq("a wrong first byte gives the uniform error", "error: invalid signature", CheckRequest(dojoKey, "GET /orders", dojoEarly));
Dojo.Eq("a wrong last byte gives the same error", "error: invalid signature", CheckRequest(dojoKey, "GET /orders", dojoLate));
Dojo.Eq("a short tag gives the same error", "error: invalid signature", CheckRequest(dojoKey, "GET /orders", dojoTag[..10]));
hints: `FixedTimeEquals` already returns false for different lengths, so the length check can go.
One `return` with a conditional: `ok` or the single error text.
